'''Mount Rainier''' ({{IPAc-en|r|eɪ|ˈ|n|ɪər}} {{respell|ray|NEER}}), also known as '''Tahoma''' ({{IPAc-en|t|ə|ˈ|h|oʊ|m|ə}} {{respell|tə|HOH|mə}}),{{efn|Indigenous peoples around the mountain have names for it in their languages:
* {{Langx|lut|təqʷubəʔ}} and {{Langx|lut|xʷaq̓ʷ|label=none}}<ref name="Tulalip Place Names2"/><ref name="Bright2"/>
* {{Langx|cow|təx̣ʷúma}} and {{Lang|cow|təqʷúmen}}<ref name="CowlitzDic"/>
* {{Langx|yak|Tax̱úma}}<ref name="Beavert2009"/>}} is a large, active [[stratovolcano]] in the [[Cascade Range]] of the [[Pacific Northwest]] in the United States. The mountain is located in [[Mount Rainier National Park]] about {{convert|59|mi|km|0}} south-southeast of [[Seattle]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Egan |first=Timothy |author-link=Timothy Egan |date=August 22, 1999 |title=Respecting Mount Rainier |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/08/22/travel/respecting-mount-rainier.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=March 10, 2022 |archive-date=March 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220311075006/https://www.nytimes.com/1999/08/22/travel/respecting-mount-rainier.html |url-status=live}}</ref> At 14,406{{nbsp}}ft{{efn| Before 2014, Mount Rainier's icecap at the Columbia Crest was the highest point on the mountain, and was surveyed at {{convert|14,410|ft}} in 1956.<ref name=Gilbertson/> Due to [[climate change]], the Columbia Crest has melted down to a height of {{convert|14,394.6|ft|m}}, while Mount Rainier's Southwest Rim was measured at {{convert|14,406.3|ft|m}},<ref name=Beason/> which would make it the new highest point on the volcano.<ref>{{cite news |title=Mount Rainier is shrinking and now has a new summit |first1=Conrad |last1=Swanson |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/climate-lab/mount-rainier-is-shrinking-and-now-has-a-new-summit/ |access-date=4 February 2025 |work=The Seattle Times |date=6 October 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.newsweek.com/washingtons-tallest-mountain-shrinking-age-mount-rainier-1966278 |title=Washington's Tallest Mountain is Shrinking With Age |first1=Tom |last1=Howarth |website=[[Newsweek]] |date=October 9, 2024 |access-date=October 17, 2024 |archive-date=October 10, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241010010451/https://www.newsweek.com/washingtons-tallest-mountain-shrinking-age-mount-rainier-1966278 |url-status=live}}</ref>}} ({{convert|14,406|ft|disp=out}}) it is the highest mountain in the U.S. state of [[Washington (state)|Washington]], the most [[Topographic prominence|topographically prominent]] mountain in the [[contiguous United States]],<ref name="NGeo-Bisharat">{{cite web |last=Bisharat |first=Andrew |date=October 3, 2018 |title=Navigating Mount Rainier's deadly ice caves for science |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/mount-rainier-washington-ice-cave-exploration-danger-discovery |work=[[National Geographic]] |access-date=October 16, 2024 |archive-date=February 5, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240205030836/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/mount-rainier-washington-ice-cave-exploration-danger-discovery |url-status=live}}</ref> and the tallest in the [[Cascade Volcanic Arc]].

Due to its high probability of an eruption in the near future and proximity to a [[Seattle metropolitan area|major urban area]], Mount Rainier is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, and it is on the [[Decade Volcano]] list.<ref>{{cite web archived |url=https://vulcan.wr.usgs.gov/Volcanoes/DecadeVolcanoes/framework.html |archive-date=June 3, 2012 |title=Decade Volcanoes |work=CVO |publisher=United States Geological Survey }}</ref> The large amount of glacial ice means that Mount Rainier could produce massive [[lahar]]s that could threaten the entire [[Puyallup River]] valley and other river valleys draining Mount Rainier, including the [[Carbon River|Carbon]], [[White River (Puyallup River)|White]], [[Nisqually River|Nisqually]], and [[Cowlitz River|Cowlitz]] (above [[Riffe Lake]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Volcanic Hazards at Mount Rainier |url=https://www.usgs.gov/volcanoes/mount-rainier/science/volcanic-hazards-mount-rainier |publisher=U.S. Geological Survey |access-date=March 22, 2024}}</ref> According to the [[United States Geological Survey]]'s 2008 report, "about 80,000 people and their homes are at risk in Mount Rainier's lahar-hazard zones."<ref name="Driedger">{{cite web |last1=Driedger |first1=C.L. |last2=Scott |first2=K.M. |date=2008 |title=Mount Rainier – Learning to Live with Volcanic Risk |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2008/3062/fs2008-3062.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090511190734/http://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2008/3062/fs2008-3062.pdf |archive-date=May 11, 2009 |access-date=October 30, 2008 |work=Fact Sheet 034-02 |publisher=United States Geological Survey |url-status=live}}</ref>

Between 1950 and 2022, 471,792 people attempted to climb Mount Rainier according to NPS statistics.<ref name="14 June 2022">{{cite journal |author1=Emma P. DeLoughery |author2=Thomas G. DeLoughery |date=June 14, 2022 |title=Review and Analysis of Mountaineering Accidents in the United States from 1947–2018 |url=https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/full/10.1089/ham.2021.0085#B8 |journal=High Altitude Medicine & Biology |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=114–118 |doi=10.1089/ham.2021.0085 |pmid=35263173 |s2cid=247361980 |access-date=July 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711104944/https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/full/10.1089/ham.2021.0085 |archive-date=July 11, 2022 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="nps-cl_stats">{{cite web |date=January 17, 2023 |title=Annual Climbing Statistics |url=https://www.nps.gov/mora/planyourvisit/annual-climbing-statistics.htm |publisher=National Park Service |access-date=July 11, 2022 |archive-date=July 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711103544/https://www.nps.gov/mora/planyourvisit/annual-climbing-statistics.htm |url-status=live}}</ref> Approximately 84 people died in mountaineering accidents on Mount Rainier from 1947 to 2018.<ref name="14 June 2022"/>

==Name==
[[File:Mt Rainier from ISS 2018.jpg|thumb|left|Mount Rainier seen from the [[International Space Station]]]]

The many [[Indigenous peoples]] who have lived near Mount Rainier for millennia have many names for the mountain in their [[Pacific Northwest languages|various languages]]. A linguistic analysis published in 2025 identified 20 indigenous names for the mountain.<ref>{{cite news |last=Board |first=Conner |date=March 13, 2025 |title=Puyallup Tribe seeks to restore Mount Rainier's original name through linguistic research |url=https://www.king5.com/article/news/community/facing-race/new-paper-analyzes-many-names-mount-rainier/281-a9d7b9de-d2d2-4afc-a258-9592082bfe17 |publisher=[[KING-TV|KING 5 News]] |access-date=March 14, 2025}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | author=Puyallup Tribe | date=February 24, 2025 |title=Puyallup Tribal language consultant publishes first comprehensive analysis of the many Native names for Mount Rainier – ʔuhuyəxʷ ti dᶻixʷ pipa ʔə tiiɫ qa sda |url=https://www.puyalluptribe-nsn.gov/news/puyallup-tribal-language-consultant-publishes-first-comprehensive-analysis-of-the-many-native-names-for-mount-rainier-%CA%94uhuy%C9%99x%CA%B7-ti-d%E1%B6%BBix%CA%B7-pipa-%CA%94%C9%99-tii%C9%AB-qa-sda/ | publisher=Puyallup Tribe of Indians | access-date=February 25, 2026}}</ref>

[[Lushootseed]] speakers have several names for Mount Rainier, including {{Langx|lut|xʷaq̓ʷ|label=none}}<ref name="Tulalip Place Names2">{{Cite web |title=Puget Sound Geographical names |url=https://tulaliplushootseed.com/places/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220404195058/https://tulaliplushootseed.com/places/ |archive-date=2022-04-04 |access-date=April 24, 2026 |publisher=Tulalip Tribes of Washington}}</ref> and {{Langx|lut|təqʷubəʔ|label=none}}.<ref name="Tulalip Place Names2" /> {{Langx|lut|xʷaq̓ʷ|label=none}} means "sky wiper" or "one who touches the sky" in English.<ref name="Tulalip Place Names2" /> The word ''{{Langx|lut|təqʷubəʔ|label=none}}'' means "snow-covered mountain".<ref name="Tulalip Place Names2" /><ref name="Bright2">{{cite book |last1=Bright |first1=William |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5XfxzCm1qa4C&q=tacoma |title=Native American Placenames of the United States |date=2004 |publisher=University of Oklahoma Press |isbn=0-8061-3576-X |page=469 |access-date=May 10, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224082306/https://books.google.com.pk/books?id=5XfxzCm1qa4C&q=tacoma&redir_esc=y#v=snippet&q=tacoma&f=false |archive-date=February 24, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> ''{{Langx|lut|təqʷubəʔ|label=none}}'' has been anglicized in many ways, including "Tacoma" and "Tacobet".<ref>{{cite news |last=Longoria |first=Ruth |date=September 26, 1999 |title=Puget hits the shore |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/97375155/puget-hits-the-shore/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220311075006/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/97375155/puget-hits-the-shore/ |archive-date=March 11, 2022 |access-date=March 10, 2022 |work=[[The Olympian]] |page=A12 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

[[Cowlitz language|Cowlitz]] speakers call the mountain {{Lang|cow|təx̣ʷúma}} or {{Lang|cow|təqʷúmen}}.<ref name="CowlitzDic">{{Cite web |title=Cowlitz Salish Dictionary |url=https://dictionary.cowlitzsalish.org/#/E/mount%20rainier |access-date=June 4, 2024 |website=[[Cowlitz Indian Tribe]] |archive-date=June 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604182037/https://dictionary.cowlitzsalish.org/#/E/mount%20rainier |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Sahaptin language|Sahaptin]] speakers call the mountain ''{{Lang|yak|Tax̱úma}}'', which is borrowed from Cowlitz.<ref name="Beavert2009">{{Cite book |last1=Beavert |first1=Virginia |author-link=Virginia Beavert |title=Ichishkíin Sɨ́nwit: Yakama/Yakima Sahaptin Dictionary |last2=Hargus |first2=Sharon |publisher=[[Heritage University]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-295-98915-0 |location=Toppenish |pages=209–210 |oclc=1299328956}}</ref>

Another anglicized name is Pooskaus.<ref>{{cite news |last=Banse |first=Tom |date=February 7, 2012 |title=Is it time to rename Mount Rainier to its former native name? |url=http://www.kplu.org/post/it-time-rename-mount-rainier-its-former-native-name |publisher=KPLU |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021035212/http://www.kplu.org/post/it-time-rename-mount-rainier-its-former-native-name |archive-date=October 21, 2014}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=What language is this supposed to be?|date=September 2024}}

[[George Vancouver]] named Mount Rainier in honor of his friend, Rear Admiral [[Peter Rainier (Royal Navy officer, born 1741)|Peter Rainier]].<ref name="npsNatureNotes">{{cite journal |title=Historical Notes: Vancouver's Voyage |journal=Mount Rainier Nature Notes |url=http://npshistory.com/nature_notes/mora/vol7/vol7-14e.htm |volume=VII |issue=14 |year=1929 |access-date=February 3, 2015 |archive-date=January 17, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117211728/http://npshistory.com/nature_notes/mora/vol7/vol7-14e.htm |url-status=live}}</ref> The [[:File:Map of Lewis and Clark's Track, Across the Western Portion of North America, published 1814.jpg|map of the Lewis and Clark expedition]] of 1804–1806 refers to it as "Mt. Regniere". Although Rainier had been considered the official name of the mountain, [[Theodore Winthrop]] referred to the mountain as "Tacoma" in his posthumously published 1862 travel book ''The Canoe and the Saddle''. For a time, both names were used interchangeably, although residents of the nearby city of [[Tacoma, Washington|Tacoma]] preferred Mount Tacoma.<ref name="Catton">{{cite book |last=Catton |first=Theodore |title=National Park, City Playground: Mount Rainier in the Twentieth Century |series=A Samuel and Althea Stroum Book |date=2006 |publisher=University of Washington Press |location=Seattle and London |isbn=0-295-98643-3 |pages=8–9}}</ref><ref name="Winthrop">{{cite book |last=Winthrop |first=Theodore |author-link=Theodore Winthrop |title=The canoe and the saddle: adventures among the northwestern rivers and forests, and Isthmiana |url=http://memory.loc.gov/cgi-bin/query/r?ammem/mymhiwebib:@field(NUMBER+@band(mymhiwe+f891w56)): |access-date=March 4, 2009 |edition=8th |orig-date=1866 |publisher=Ticknor and Fields |location=Boston |chapter=VII. Tacoma |chapter-url=http://memory.loc.gov/cgi-bin/ampage?collId=mymhiwe&fileName=f891w56/mymhiwef891w56.db&recNum=121&itemLink=r?ammem/mymhiwe:@field(DOCID+@lit(mymhiwef891w56div7))%23f891w56122&linkText=1 |isbn=0-665-37762-2 |archive-date=February 24, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224082118/http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/index.html |url-status=live}}</ref><!-- note that this ISBN number comes back as the 10th edition (and in microform), not the 8th cited here -->

In 1890, the [[United States Board on Geographic Names]] declared that the mountain would be known as Rainier.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Orth |first=Donald J. |year=1992 |title=The Creation |page=18 |journal=Meridian |publisher=Map and Geospatial Information Round Table |issue=2 |url=https://geonames.usgs.gov/docs/Proceedings%20of%20a%20Centennial%20Symposium.pdf |oclc=18508074 |access-date=August 31, 2015 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304230452/http://geonames.usgs.gov/docs/Proceedings%20of%20a%20Centennial%20Symposium.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> Following this in 1897, the Pacific Forest Reserve became the [[Rainier National Forest|Mount Rainier Forest Reserve]], and the national park was established three years later. Despite this, there was still a movement to change the mountain's name to Tacoma, and Congress was considering a resolution to change the name as late as 1924.<ref>{{cite news |last=Blethen |first=C. B. |date=February 3, 1924 |title=Academic Dispute Flares Forth; Mount Rainier's Name at Issue |newspaper=The Seattle Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |date=September 1917 |title=The Outdoor World: Mt. Rainier's Name Stands |page=142 |magazine=Recreation |publisher=Outdoor World Publishing Company |volume=LVII |issue=3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gX87AQAAMAAJ |via=Google Books |oclc=12010285 |access-date=August 31, 2015}}</ref>

==Geographical setting==
[[File:Rainier Aerial West Close Washington Mar23 R16 07149.jpg|thumb|West face of Mount Rainier from an aircraft]]

Mount Rainier is the tallest mountain in Washington and the Cascade Range. This peak is located southeast of Tacoma, approximately {{convert|60|mi|km}} south-southeast of Seattle.<ref>{{cite web |last=McRoberts |first=Patrick |date=March 2, 2003 |title=U.S. Congress creates Mount Rainier National Park on March 2, 1899. |url=https://www.historylink.org/File/5345 |work=[[HistoryLink]] |access-date=October 16, 2024 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007164054/https://www.historylink.org/File/5345 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |date=August 16, 2024 |title=Mount Rainier |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Mount-Rainier |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] |access-date=October 16, 2024}}</ref> Mount Rainier has a [[topographic prominence]] of {{convert|13210|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}.<ref name="NGeo-Bisharat"/> On clear days it dominates the southeastern horizon in most of the [[Seattle metropolitan area|Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area]] to such an extent that locals sometimes refer to it simply as "the Mountain".<ref name="barcott">{{cite web archived |url=http://www.ac.wwu.edu/~bgoebel/members/bbarcott.htm |archive-date=January 13, 2009 |title=The Mountain is Out |access-date=March 23, 2007 |first1=Bruce |last1=Barcott |date=April 27, 1999 |publisher= |author-link=Bruce Barcott}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=September 4, 2019 |title=Image of the Day: Mount Rainier |url=https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/145548/mount-rainier |publisher=[[NASA Earth Observatory]] |access-date=November 23, 2024}}</ref> On days of exceptional clarity, it can also be seen from as far away as [[Corvallis, Oregon]] (at [[Marys Peak]]), and the [[North Shore Mountains]] in [[British Columbia]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Hale |first=Jamie |date=April 29, 2017 |title=A 10-mountain view on top of Marys Peak, the best viewpoint in Oregon |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/travel/2017/04/a_10-mountain_view_on_top_of_m.html |work=[[The Oregonian]] |access-date=November 23, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Emrick |first=Larry |date=July 19, 1986 |title=Mt. Rainier: on top of the world |page=D2 |work=[[Vancouver Sun]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-vancouver-sun-mt-rainier-on-top-of/159617504/ |via=Newspapers.com |access-date=November 23, 2024}}</ref>

With 26 major [[glacier]]s<ref name=cvo-glacier>{{cite web |title=Mount Rainier Glaciers and Glaciations |url=https://vulcan.wr.usgs.gov/Volcanoes/Rainier/Glaciers/description_rainier_glaciers.html |first=Lyn |last=Topinka |year=2002 |publisher=United States Geological Survey |access-date=April 22, 2010 |archive-date=December 26, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226111437/https://volcanoes.usgs.gov/volcanoes/mount_rainier/mount_rainier_geo_hist_77.html |url-status=live}}</ref> and {{convert|36|sqmi|abbr=on}} of permanent [[snowfield]]s and glaciers,<ref name=Driedger-glacier/> Mount Rainier is the most heavily [[glaciated]] peak in the lower 48 states. The summit is topped by two [[volcanic crater]]s, each more than {{convert|1000|ft|m|-2|abbr=on}} in diameter, with the larger east crater overlapping the west crater. [[Geothermal (geology)|Geothermal]] heat from the [[volcano]] keeps areas of both crater rims free of snow and ice, and the world's largest volcanic [[glacier cave]] network has formed within the ice-filled craters,<ref name="Zimbelman2000">{{cite journal |last1=Zimbelman |first1=D.R. |last2=Rye |first2=R.O. |last3=Landis |first3=G.P. |title=Fumaroles in ice caves on the summit of Mount Rainier: Preliminary stable isotope, gas, and geochemical studies |journal=Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research |volume=97 |issue=1–4 |pages=457–473 |year=2000 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0273(99)00180-8 |bibcode=2000JVGR...97..457Z |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1260041 |access-date=June 28, 2019 |archive-date=March 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326001346/https://zenodo.org/record/1260041 |url-status=live}}</ref> with nearly {{convert|2|mi|km|abbr=on}} of passages.<ref>{{cite news |title=Exploring Rainier's summit steam caves |author=Sandi Doughton |newspaper=The News Tribune |date=October 25, 2007 |url=http://www.thenewstribune.com/2007/10/08/174171/exploring-rainiers-summit-steam.html |access-date=October 3, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120905080031/http://www.thenewstribune.com/2007/10/08/174171/exploring-rainiers-summit-steam.html |archive-date=September 5, 2012}}</ref>
A small [[Volcanic crater lake|crater lake]] about {{convert|130|by|30|ft|m|abbr=on}} in size and {{Convert|16|ft|m|0|abbr=on}} deep, the highest in North America with a surface elevation of {{convert|14203|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, occupies the lowest portion of the west crater below more than {{convert|100|ft|m|-1|abbr=on}} of ice and is accessible only via the caves.<ref name="Kiver1971">{{cite journal |last1=Kiver |first1=Eugene P. |last2=Mumma |first2=Martin D. |title=Summit Firn Caves, Mount Rainier, Washington |journal=Science |volume=173 |issue=3994 |pages=320–322 |year=1971 |doi=10.1126/science.173.3994.320 |pmid=17809214 |bibcode=1971Sci...173..320K |s2cid=21323576}}</ref><ref name="Kiver1975">{{cite journal |last1=Kiver |first1=Eugene P. |last2=Steele |first2=William K. |title=Firn Caves in the Volcanic Craters of Mount Rainier, Washington |journal=The NSS Bulletin |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=45–55 |year=1975 |url=http://legacy.caves.org/pub/journal/PDF/V37/v37n3-Kiver.htm |access-date=November 14, 2008 |archive-date=January 16, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116171026/http://caves.org/pub/journal/PDF/V37/v37n3-Kiver.htm |url-status=live}}</ref>

The [[Carbon River|Carbon]], [[Cowlitz River|Cowlitz]], [[Nisqually River|Nisqually]], [[Puyallup River|Puyallup]] and North [[Mowich River]]s begin at [[eponym]]ous glaciers of Mount Rainier.<ref name="Mt. Rainier Glaciers">{{cite web |title=Mount Rainier Glaciers |url=https://www.nps.gov/mora/learn/nature/mount-rainier-glaciers.htm |publisher=National Park Service |date=2023-08-18 |access-date=November 18, 2024 |archive-date=April 15, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240415160158/https://www.nps.gov/mora/learn/nature/mount-rainier-glaciers.htm |url-status=live}}</ref> The sources of the [[White River (Washington)|White River]] are [[Winthrop Glacier|Winthrop]], [[Emmons Glacier|Emmons]], and [[Fryingpan Glacier]]s.<ref name="Mt. Rainier Glaciers"/> The White, Carbon, and Mowich join the Puyallup River, which discharges into [[Commencement Bay]] at [[Tacoma, Washington|Tacoma]].<ref>{{cite report |date=June 19, 2003 |title=Geomorphic Evaluation and Channel Mitigation Zone Analysis: Puyallup, Carbon and White Rivers |page=6 |url=https://www.piercecountywa.gov/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/1158 |publisher=Pierce County Public Works and Utilities |access-date=November 25, 2024}}</ref> The Nisqually empties into Puget Sound east of [[Lacey, Washington|Lacey]].<ref name="Givens 2020">{{cite web |last=Givens |first=Linda Holden |title=Lacey -- Thumbnail History |work=HistoryLink |date=2020-09-01 |url=https://www.historylink.org/file/21095 |access-date=2024-11-25}}</ref> The Cowlitz joins the [[Columbia River]] between [[Kelso, Washington|Kelso]] and [[Longview, Washington|Longview]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Markon |first=John |date=September 28, 2013 |title=Come along for a tour of the mighty Cowlitz River |url=https://tdn.com/lifestyles/come-along-for-a-tour-of-the-mighty-cowlitz-river/article_cbd20958-27ad-11e3-aeb0-001a4bcf887a.html |work=[[The Daily News (Longview)|The Daily News]] |location=Longview, Washington |url-access=subscription |access-date=November 25, 2024}}</ref>

{{wide image|Mount Rainier 5845s.JPG|640px|A panorama of the northeast face of Mount Rainier}}
{{clear}}

===Subsidiary peaks===
[[File:Mount Rainier 22925.JPG|thumb|right|[[Little Tahoma Peak]] to the left of Mount Rainier, from [[Panhandle Gap]]]]
The broad top of Mount Rainier contains three named summits. The highest of these named summits is known as the Columbia Crest. The second-highest summit is Point Success, {{convert|14158|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, at the southern edge of the summit plateau, atop the ridge known as Success Cleaver. It has a [[topographic prominence]] of about {{convert|138|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, so it is not considered a separate peak. The lowest of the three summits is Liberty Cap, {{convert|14112|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, at the northwestern edge, which overlooks Liberty Ridge, the Sunset Amphitheater, and the dramatic [[Willis Wall]].<ref>Named after [[Bailey Willis]], USGS geological engineer, who played a key role in getting Mount Rainier designated as a national park. {{cite book |chapter-url=http://www.cr.nps.gov/history/online_books/berkeley/rensch2/rensch2f.htm |title=Mount Rainier: Its Human History Associations |chapter=Scientific Exploration Of Mount Rainier |publisher=National Park Service |access-date=February 20, 2013 |archive-date=March 26, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070326002622/http://www.cr.nps.gov/history/online_books/berkeley/rensch2/rensch2f.htm }}</ref>

High on the eastern flank of Mount Rainier is a peak known as [[Little Tahoma Peak]], {{convert|11138|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, an eroded remnant of the earlier, much higher, Mount Rainier. It has a prominence of {{convert|858|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, and it is rarely climbed in direct conjunction with Columbia Crest, so it is usually considered a separate peak. If considered separately from Mount Rainier, Little Tahoma Peak would be the third-highest mountain peak in Washington.<ref>{{cite gnis |id=1533577 |name=Little Tahoma Peak |access-date=November 25, 2008}}</ref>

=== Height of the mountain ===
Mount Rainier was one of five historical icecap summits in the [[lower 48 states]], meaning that its elevation has changed as a result of [[glacial melting]] due to [[climate change]].<ref name=Gilbertson>{{cite journal |last1=Gilbertson |first1=Eric |last2=Abatzoglou |first2=John T. |last3=Stanchak |first3=Kathryn E. |last4=Hotaling |first4=Scott |author1-link=Eric Gilbertson (climber) |title=Rapid contemporary shrinking and loss of ice-capped summits in the western United States |journal=Arctic, Antarctic, and Alpine Research |date=2025 |volume=57 |issue=1 |article-number=2572898 |doi=10.1080/15230430.2025.2572898 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/15230430.2025.2572898?scroll=top&needAccess=true#abstract |issn=1523-0430|doi-access=free }}</ref>
The [[National Park Service]] and [[United States Geological Survey]] cite Mount Rainier's summit as the Columbia Crest icecap at {{convert|14410|ft|m|0|abbr=on}};<ref name="NPS-Icon">{{cite web |title=An Icon on the Horizon |url=https://www.nps.gov/mora/index.htm |publisher=[[National Park Service]] |access-date=October 17, 2024 |archive-date=July 20, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060720050115/http://www.nps.gov/mora/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="USGS-Volcanoes">{{Cite web |title=Mount Rainier, Washington – Summary |url=https://volcanoes.usgs.gov/observatories/cvo/Historical/LewisClark/Info/summary_mount_rainier.shtml |publisher=U.S. Geological Survey |access-date=October 17, 2024 |archive-date=October 9, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241009164104/https://volcanoes.usgs.gov/observatories/cvo/Historical/LewisClark/Info/summary_mount_rainier.shtml |url-status=live}}</ref> this value was determined in 1956, referenced to the [[National Geodetic Vertical Datum of 1929]] (NGVD29).<ref name="Signani">{{Cite news |last=Signani |first=Larry |date=July 19, 2000 |title=The Height of Accuracy |url=https://www.pobonline.com/Articles/Features/1fc6f0b5ba0f6010VgnVCM100000f932a8c0____ |work=Point of Beginning Magazine |publisher=BNP Media |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121217170809/https://www.pobonline.com/Articles/Features/1fc6f0b5ba0f6010VgnVCM100000f932a8c0____ |archive-date=December 17, 2012 |access-date=October 17, 2024}}</ref> 
In 1999, the mountain summit was surveyed at {{convert|14411|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}, also in the NGVD29.{{efn|The 1999 survey was based on the [[North American Vertical Datum of 1988]], but the result was converted to NGVD29 by the original authors for comparison to previous values.}}<ref name="Signani" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Archbold |first=Mike |date=August 12, 2010 |title=Rainier still measures up: 14,411 feet |url=https://www.theolympian.com/outdoors/article25261372.html |work=[[The Olympian]] |access-date=October 17, 2024 |quote=Finally, we converted the NAVD 88 elevations to NAVD 29 [sic, NGVD 29] elevations for comparison to previous values.}}</ref>

In the 2020s, [[Eric Gilbertson (climber)|Eric Gilbertson]] and other surveyors found that the Columbia Crest had melted down so that it was no longer the highest point on the mountain after around 2014. According to Gilbertson's research, the current summit of the mountain is a point of bare rock on the southwest crater rim at {{convert|14,399.6|ft}} +/- {{convert|3|cm|abbr=on}}. This figure also uses the NGVD29 datum.<ref name="Gilbertson" /> Mount Rainier National Park geologists expressed concerns over the methods used in the study and requested the data for evaluation, though they recorded similar glacial thinning. An official measurement taken in 2010 saw little to no change from the official value.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ryan |first=John |date=2025-11-26 |title=Mount Rainier is shrinking (just a bit), new study finds |url=https://thankyou.kuow.org/stories/mount-rainier-shrinking-just-a-little-new-study-finds |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=thankyou.kuow.org |language=en}}</ref>
